name: RADAR-001 hand-labelled ICU-monitoring slice
labelled_by: author, by reading each record's official title and abstract on 2026-11-17
labelling_rules: expected_topics lists only what the record's own title/abstract makes clear. A keyword mention is not enough.
An empty expected_topics list is deliberate: it tests whether the model abstains instead of pattern-matching a word.

expected_organization is the vendor named by the record itself (an applicant field or a vendor page). A paper affiliation is NOT an expected organisation for a product claim, so PMID items expect null.
Labels are the author's reading, not a rule layer's output. Disagreement is reported, not resolved in the model's favour.

items.rationale: Machine-learning prediction model for HFNC failure; clearly predictive modelling in critical care.
Interpretable machine-learning models predicting haemodynamic stabilization.
Prognostic prediction model for sepsis-associated acute kidney injury.
A derived ratio used to build a mortality prediction model; no device is evaluated.
Machine-learning classification model for ICU pressure injury status.
Machine-learning risk stratification model in preterm infants.
A trial protocol about haemodynamics during induction; monitoring-adjacent, not a device study.
Nursing workforce role description. It mentions deterioration but is not about a monitoring technology.
Surgical case report. Off-topic for ICU monitoring technology.
Lipid-panel equation comparison. Off-topic; a keyword matcher would wrongly fire on 'model'.
FDA 510(k) for an ELECTROCARDIOGRAPH filed by Philips Medical Systems (Cleveland).
FDA 510(k) for an ELECTROCARDIOGRAPH filed by Cambridge Instruments, which is not a monitored vendor.
Coronary imaging and physiology in the cathlab: a Philips product, but outside the ICU patient-monitoring topic set, so no topic should be asserted.

limitations: 14 items is a smoke-sized labelled set. It can detect a broken prompt or a fabrication, not establish general accuracy.
The sample is skewed towards PubMed prediction papers because that is what the PubMed queries returned; precision on off-topic records is therefore under-sampled relative to the live mix.
The author is not a clinician; labels follow the record's own wording.
